b: For consistent at-home tracking, measure at your belly button with a non-stretch tape. Stand relaxed, keep the tape level and snug, and read it after a normal exhale. If your result is within a few centimeters of a screening cutoff, recheck at the midpoint between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone before interpreting it.

Body Mass Index (BMI) is the most commonly used test to screen for obesity. While it is often criticized because it can't tell whether that weight is muscle or fat, much less where the fat is sitting, it has a much bigger problem: it misses about half of people who are carrying too much fat.1

Adding a waist circumference measurement to BMI helps with most of these problems. Because harmful fat tends to pile up in the abdomen, measuring your waist is a quick and cheap way to tell whether excess body fat might be putting your health at risk. The catch is that where you put the tape changes the number, and most people have never been shown how to do it. In this article, we'll cover why you should measure your waist, how you should do it, and what your measurement means.
Why should you measure your waist?

You should measure your waist because it estimates how much fat you're carrying around your abdomen, which your weight and BMI can't really do. This visceral fat, the fat stored around your internal organs, increases the risk of obesity-related chronic diseases like high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease, among others. By measuring your waist accurately, you're getting a quick and easy read on where the fat is, and how much of it you have.

When it comes to measuring body fat and its potential impact on health, think of a continuum running from least predictive to most. On the least predictive side, you have bodyweight. Unless someone has a very high or low body weight, any assumption about the amount and location of the fat they're carrying is just that: an assumption. One step up from weight alone is BMI, as it adds a height component, which can help make predictions about how much fat someone has, but not where it's located. Next up is waist circumference, which adds information about where the fat is.

In 359,387 European adults, every additional 5 cm of waist circumference at a given BMI was associated with 17% higher mortality in men and 13% higher in women.2 A pooled analysis of 650,386 adults found the same relationship within every BMI category from 20 to 50, so there wasn't a body size where the waist stopped adding information.3
What these data sets are capturing is that body fat's potential to cause harm rises when there is too much of it in the wrong location.

After waist circumference, there is the Body Roundness Index (BRI), which uses waist circumference and height to further characterize the amount of fat. The next step up from there would be a DXA scan, which uses X-ray technology to separate the body into three types of tissue: fat mass, bone, and lean mass. On the most predictive side, you have something like a liver biopsy, since the liver is generally where the body starts storing fat when it runs out of room to store it safely. By adding information about the amount of fat someone has stored and its location, we know more and more about its impact on health.

The people BMI misses are the ones whose weight looks fine at every checkup while their body fat says otherwise. In one analysis, 39% of adults whose BMI said they didn't have obesity turned out to have it once their body fat was actually measured.4 That's why an international consensus group has argued that waist circumference should be treated as a vital sign, even though it still isn't routinely measured in clinical practice.5
How do you measure your waist?
Wrap a non-stretch tape around your bare abdomen at the level of your belly button and read it at the end of a normal exhalation, with the tape level and snug against the skin.
Stand upright with your feet together and your arms at your sides.

Wrap the tape around your abdomen at the level of your belly button. A tailor's tape works fine. A spring-loaded tape that applies a fixed tension works better, because how hard you pull is the biggest source of error. The tape should sit against the skin without denting it, so if it presses a groove into you it's too tight, and if you can fit more than a finger under it it's too loose.
Keep the tape parallel to the floor all the way around. This is the step people get wrong most often, and a tape that rides up in the back reads low.
Don't brace, suck in, or push your belly out. Breathe normally and take the reading at the end of a normal exhale.
Measure twice. If the two readings differ by more than a centimeter, take a third and average the two closest. Record it to the nearest 0.1 cm or eighth of an inch.

Measure first thing in the morning, after using the bathroom and before eating or drinking. A big meal or menstrual-cycle fluid shifts can change the number by about as much as a month of real progress. Once a week is plenty, since daily measurements are mostly noise. While there's some degree of error with self measurement, the error is fairly constant for any one person, so you can use the numbers to track your own change over time.5
Where should you measure your waist?
For measuring yourself at home, we recommend measuring at the belly button. That isn't the site most guidelines use, so it helps to know what the options are.

At least eight different measurement sites show up in the research literature, and a 2020 international consensus statement concluded that the protocols recommended by leading health organizations have no scientific rationale behind them.5, 6 Three sites dominate:
The midpoint between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, used by the World Health Organization.
The top of the hip bone (the iliac crest), used by the National Institutes of Health and the NHANES survey that produces most American data.7
The belly button (umbilicus), used by about 29% of the waist circumference literature.5

Fortunately, where you measure doesn't really change what the number predicts. A systematic review of 120 studies found that the link between waist circumference and heart disease, diabetes, and death held up regardless of which protocol was used.8 However, the site used does change the number itself. In men the hip bone and midpoint sites read about the same, but in women the hip bone site runs about 2 cm higher in Western samples and up to 9 cm higher in one Japanese sample.9, 10 The belly button reads higher still. In 97 postmenopausal women with obesity, the average reading was 108.3 cm at the midpoint and 115.7 cm at the belly button.11

So why the belly button? People tend to find it easier to locate than the bony landmarks, which makes it more repeatable.12 In one study, measurements taken by different people varied about half as much at the belly button as at the midpoint.11 In that study, the narrowest point was as repeatable as the belly button and tracked visceral fat better, but trained researchers found it by looking at the torso from behind. On yourself, and especially with extra belly fat, there often isn’t a clear narrowest point, so we’d rather you use a landmark you can find the same way every time.

Finding your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone means pressing into tissue, and that gets more challenging in those with obesity. While the midpoint measurement seems to correlate better with MRI-measured visceral fat compared to measuring at the belly button, the differences aren't big enough to really matter.11 I think a slightly weaker correlation is a fair price for a measurement that you can take easily and reliably.

Find the bottom rib and top of the hip bone.

If you'd rather use the midpoint, find the bottom edge of your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone on one side and mark the halfway point. Do the same on the other side so the tape has something to line up with. If you use the hip bone (iliac crest) site, the landmark is the uppermost edge of the hip bone at your side, in line with your armpit. That's a different spot from the bony point at the front of your pelvis, which is a common mistake.7

Waist circumference measures the fat under your skin and the fat inside your abdomen together, along with your abdominal wall and whatever is in your gut. While imperfect, the waist measurement is the easiest way to measure if fat is ending up someplace it shouldn't be, which raises the question of where does body fat go in the first place?
Body fat is stored in two general locations:
Subcutaneous fat is the layer under your skin that you can pinch. It's your main storage depot, where we store fat safely as long as it has room.
Ectopic fat is the fat stored outside that depot. It includes visceral fat, which is packed around the organs inside your abdomen. It also includes fat inside the liver, pancreas, heart, and muscle.

The tape correlates moderately with visceral fat (r = 0.4 to 0.6), depending on the site and the population.5 That means the tape and an MRI, which is very precise, agree on who's at the extremes. They sometimes disagree about the people in the middle.

Visceral fat and the other ectopic fat depots are where most of the metabolic damage of excess body fat happens, and we cover why in Why Your Waist Matters More Than Your Weight. How much fat ends up there depends a lot on how much room your subcutaneous fat has, which is where the personal fat threshold comes in.
What is the personal fat threshold?

The personal fat threshold is the amount of body fat a particular person can store safely before fat starts spilling into the liver and pancreas and driving metabolic disease like type 2 diabetes.13 That amount varies from person to person and it doesn't line up neatly with BMI or body weight.

Think of your subcutaneous fat tissue as a garage. Inside, fat is stored as boxes, with each box being energy you took in and didn't burn. Storing boxes is what the garage is for. Some people have a two-car garage, some have a one-car garage, and others have virtually no garage at all. The size of your garage is mostly decided before you have any say in it. When the garage fills up, boxes start going into places they shouldn't be: the hallway, then the kitchen, then onto the stairs. In your body those are the liver, the pancreas, and your muscles, to name a few.

A liver or muscle cell that's already holding more fuel (in the form of fat) than it can use stops responding to insulin, which normally tells that cell to bring energy inside. This lack of response is insulin resistance at the level of a single cell. That's why two people can carry the same amount of fat with one of them perfectly healthy and the other developing diabetes. It's also why some lean individuals can develop diabetes: they've gone past their personal fat threshold.

The data back this up. Much of what we know about type 2 diabetes comes from the UK Prospective Diabetes Study. The median BMI at diagnosis in that cohort was 28, and one in three participants had a BMI under 25.13 A 2023 trial put the idea to a direct test in 20 people with type 2 diabetes and a BMI under 27, which describes about one in six people at diagnosis.14 After a median initial weight loss of 6.5%, 70% of them went into sustained remission off all diabetes medication. Their average BMI went from 24.8 to 22.5, and their liver fat dropped back to normal. Their waists went from 90.0 cm to 79.7 cm, and visceral fat fell 37.4% compared with 26.5% for subcutaneous fat.14 The group started with an average BMI below the standard overweight cutoff, and changes in waist circumference accompanied the reductions in body fat.

As of this writing, no measurement can find your personal threshold directly. That includes the waist measurement too. Fat in the liver can build up while your waist is still in the normal range, which is why lean people get diagnosed with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, the current name for fatty liver disease) and type 2 diabetes. The waist cutoffs below represent where risk of obesity-related chronic disease seems to be significant on average, though some individuals will experience risk at higher or lower points, which is the personal fat threshold in a nutshell.
What is a healthy waist circumference?

For most adults of European descent, a healthy waist is under 94 cm (37 in) for men and 80 cm (31.5 in) for women, and for everyone it's under half your height. The circumference cutoffs come from a 1995 study of about 1,900 adults in Glasgow, which proposed two "action levels" instead of a single cutoff.15
Action level 1 is 94 cm (37 in) for men and 80 cm (31.5 in) for women. Above this, losing fat is likely to improve your health.
Action level 2 is 102 cm (40 in) for men and 88 cm (35 in) for women. Above this, I'd recommend losing weight.

These cutoffs came from measurements at or near the rib-to-hip midpoint, and a belly button reading usually runs a bit higher, especially with more belly fat. If your belly button number lands within a few centimeters of a cutoff, re-measure at the midpoint before deciding what it means, and keep tracking at the belly button either way.

The original authors said people above action level 1 should avoid gaining more weight, but I think fat loss is likely to help at both levels.15 In a Dutch sample of about 4,900 adults, men between the two action levels had roughly double the odds of having at least one cardiovascular risk factor. Men above action level 2 had about four and a half times the odds. For women the odds were about 60% higher between the levels and about two and a half times higher above action level 2.16 Both sets of numbers are cutoffs drawn from a single population, and risk climbs steadily as the waist grows, so I'd treat them as decision points and not as a line where danger suddenly starts.

These thresholds don't fit everyone equally. For example, the values that best identify cardiovascular risk range from 80 to 98 cm in men and 80 to 96 cm in women across different ethnic groups.5 If you’re a man of South or East Asian descent, 94 cm understates your risk, and most Asian guidelines use 85 to 90 cm instead, for the same reason the WHO recommends acting at a lower BMI in those populations.17 For women, most of those guidelines use 75–80 cm, though cutoffs vary by guideline.5

Waist-to-height ratio avoids most of that. A meta-analysis found it better than either waist circumference or BMI at identifying cardiometabolic risk, and a review of 78 studies landed on 0.5 as a reasonable boundary across sexes and ethnic groups.18, 19 It's one of the reasons we use it in the Barbell Medicine Vital 5. For adults with a BMI below 35, NICE classifies ratios from 0.4 to 0.49 as healthy central adiposity.

If you already have a condition linked to excess fat, the action levels don't really apply to you. That includes prediabetes, high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, and MASLD. If you have one of these conditions, a clinician can help you interpret your waist measurement alongside your other health markers.
How do you reduce your waist circumference?

Weight loss is the most reliable way to reduce your waist circumference, because the tape mostly reads the fat under your skin and that fat comes off as you lose weight. Waist reductions reliably come with visceral fat reductions, but because the waist measurement also includes subcutaneous fat, the abdominal muscles, and what's in your gut, the size of the waist change only loosely predicts how much visceral fat you lost.5, 20 What's more, the visceral fat compartment typically contains about 10% of a person's total body fat, making it a relatively small pool. This makes interventions that reduce visceral fat appear less effective when waist circumference is the key measurement of success.
Exercise reduces visceral fat even without weight loss, though it changes your waist measurement less than you might expect.21
Aerobic training is one of the best ways to reduce visceral fat, though the changes in waist circumference are often modest.

Without any change in diet, a meta-analysis of 15 trials found that aerobic training reduced visceral fat area on CT scans by more than 30 cm2 in women and 40 cm2 in men, even in programs as short as 12 weeks.22 Another meta-analysis found that aerobic training reduced visceral fat compared with no exercise, while resistance training alone didn't.23

In one randomized trial of 300 adults, doubling the amount of aerobic exercise didn't produce any additional waist reduction, and every exercise group lost about 5 cm compared with the control group.24 A trial in postmenopausal women comparing different exercise doses found the same pattern.25 So if you're training hard and your waist isn't budging much, that doesn't mean the training isn't working when it comes to improving your health.

Resistance training helps reduce waist circumference over time, and it helps you keep the muscle you'd otherwise lose in a Calorie deficit. In about 10,500 men followed for 12 years, adding 20 minutes a day of weight training was associated with about 0.67 cm less age-related waist gain. The same time spent on aerobic exercise was associated with 0.33 cm less.26 Keeping muscle matters here because muscle is where a large share of the glucose you eat gets used.

Doing both aerobic and resistance training gave the best results for both waist circumference and body weight in that same group of men.26 Aerobic exercise alone did better for body weight than weight training did, which is roughly what you'd expect if lifting adds muscle while fat comes off. This is observational data, so it can't prove cause and effect, but the size and length of the study make it more than suggestive.

GLP-1 medications reduce waist circumference about as much as anything short of surgery. In a body composition substudy of the SURMOUNT-1 trial, 72 weeks of tirzepatide reduced waist circumference by 18.1 cm against 3.4 cm on placebo, and it cut visceral fat by 40.1% against 7.3% in the placebo group.27 In a head-to-head trial, tirzepatide reduced waist circumference by 18.4 cm compared with 13.0 cm for semaglutide.28

You've probably heard that these drugs cost you a lot of muscle. In the semaglutide trials, about 38% to 39% of the weight lost showed up as "lean mass" on DXA scans.29 DXA lumps muscle together with water, organ tissue, and the non-fat parts of fat tissue itself, so that number overstates actual muscle loss. In a 2026 trial of adults aged 50 to 70 taking tirzepatide with or without supervised lifting three days a week, the people who didn't lift lost 4.7 kg of lean tissue on DXA, 3.5 kg of it from the arms and legs. Since roughly 70% of the lean tissue in the arms and legs is skeletal muscle, the authors estimated that came to about 2.5 kg of actual muscle. The people who lifted lost 3.6 kg of lean tissue, or about 2 kg of muscle by the same math, and they got roughly 11% to 18% stronger while the non-lifters got 6% to 9% weaker.30 We cover this in more depth in GLP-1s and Muscle Loss: What the Evidence Shows.

None of this changes the recommendations to eat enough protein and do some resistance training. Virtually any type of weight loss that goes beyond water weight increases the odds of losing muscle. Some of it is unavoidable, since a larger person who loses weight is now carrying around less mass than before, which means less muscular force production in their day-to-day life. It’s almost like going from a 1.5g environment (1.5 times the normal force of Earth’s gravity) to 1g.
How fast should your waist change?

Waist change follows weight loss, especially after the initial 1-2 week phase where the loss of water weight predominates. Similarly, the greater the loss of lean mass, the more weight loss we expect per unit change in waist measurement.

As a rough guide, a good target is about 2 cm off your waist for every kilogram of weight lost, or 0.4 to 0.6 kg per centimeter. If you’re losing more than about 1 kg per centimeter of waist reduction over 8 to 12 weeks, it may be worth reviewing how your strength, nutrition, and training are changing. The ratio alone cannot tell you how much muscle you’ve lost. Expect the ratio to run higher early on in women, who tend to lose fat from the hips and thighs first, and with large, relatively fast weight loss like on GLP-1 medications.
Protein intake: should be ~ 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day
Calorie deficit: should target ~ 400-500 Calorie deficit unless there is a reason to lose faster
Resistance training: should be lifting 2-3 times per week at minimum

Weight and waist changes are rarely linear, but small changes still matter. Each additional centimeter of waist circumference is associated with about a 2% higher relative risk of cardiovascular events.31
Knowing your number is easier than deciding what to do about it, especially if you want to keep getting great results from your training without losing the muscle you've built.
